commentary: Aristotle opens by declaring that there is a science whose object is being as being, not this or that restricted portion of being, as the particular sciences study. Aquinas explains that every particular science - mathematics, natural philosophy - cuts off some segment of reality and investigates only the properties peculiar to that segment; none of them asks what belongs to a thing simply because it is a being at all. This new science, then, must have being itself as its subject, and must consider not only that subject but whatever attaches to it in its own right, per se, rather than merely incidentally. Aquinas draws an analogy to geometry: the geometer does not care whether a triangle happens to be made of bronze or wood, only with what follows necessarily from its being triangular; likewise the metaphysician sets aside what merely happens to belong to things and confines himself to what follows from being as such. He further connects this to the ancient search for first principles and highest causes: whoever sought the ultimate elements of things was implicitly seeking the principles of being as being, since nothing is more universal than being itself. Hence the science that investigates first causes and the science that investigates being qua being turn out to be one and the same undertaking - this is the long-sought science that the whole treatise calls first philosophy or wisdom, and Aristotle here simply establishes that it exists and names its proper subject.

Aquinas reads this long chapter as showing, step by step, exactly what being as being covers and why a single science can treat so vast a subject. He begins from Aristotle's illustration involving the word healthy: diet, medicine, urine, and a living body are all called healthy, yet not in one identical sense - the diet preserves health, the medicine produces it, the urine signals it, the body possesses it. These different senses are nevertheless all ordered toward one reference point, health itself. Aquinas calls this pattern analogical predication, distinct both from univocal predication, where a term keeps one shared meaning, and from pure equivocation, where meanings are unrelated. Being works the same way: substance, quantity, quality, motion, privation, and negation are all called beings, but only because each bears some relation to substance, which is being in the primary sense. Because one science can study everything ordered toward a single primary term, first philosophy can study all these modes together, though its principal concern remains substance. Aquinas then shows that being and one name the same reality under different aspects - convertible terms, unity adding only the note of undividedness to being - and concludes that wherever being has distinct species, such as substance, quantity, and quality, unity has corresponding species, such as sameness, equality, and likeness. Since one science studies a subject together with its essential attributes, and since plurality, sameness, otherness, and contrariety all flow necessarily from being and unity, the philosopher must examine these together with the negations and privations bound up with them. Aquinas also explains how dialectic and sophistic each imitate philosophy's universal reach, dialectic by arguing probably about everything and sophistic by merely appearing wise, and takes this resemblance as confirming that being itself is truly the philosopher's proper and singular subject.

Aquinas takes Aristotle's question here to be whether the axioms employed in every demonstration, and above all the principle that a thing cannot both be and not be in the same respect at once, belong to this same universal science or fall instead to some more restricted discipline, such as mathematics, which relies on them constantly. He argues that since these axioms hold true of everything that is, without being confined to any single genus of being, they must belong to whoever studies being universally, namely the metaphysician; the particular sciences merely borrow and apply them within their own limited subject matter, never pausing to demonstrate them. Aquinas notes that certain natural philosophers wrongly took themselves to be the final authorities on such principles, mistakenly supposing that changeable, natural substance was the whole of reality; but because metaphysics considers a wider and higher kind of being than physics does, it is metaphysics, not physics, that has the truer claim to examine these common truths. Aquinas then identifies the principle of non-contradiction as the firmest of all such axioms, and explains why: no one can genuinely be deceived about it, since deception occurs only where something is not already known; it does not rest on any prior supposition, since it must be possessed by anyone who understands anything whatsoever; and it arises naturally within the intellect, through the mere grasp of the terms involved, rather than through acquired demonstration. Every other axiom, and indeed every act of reasoning, ultimately rests upon it as its final and most certain foundation.

Here Aristotle confronts those who, following Heraclitus and others, hold that contradictory statements can be true of the same subject at the same time. Aquinas insists that this claim cannot be demonstrated false in the strict sense, since any such demonstration would already presuppose the very principle under dispute; instead Aristotle proceeds refutatively, forcing the opponent into self-contradiction, on the sole condition that the opponent's words mean something definite. Aquinas traces several distinct lines of attack in turn. First, if a name like man signifies one definite thing, then to be a man cannot also be to be a non-man, since a thing cannot simultaneously possess and lack its own defining essence; this shows that predication must sometimes be essential and not merely accidental, since purely accidental predication running to infinity would leave nothing fixed to talk about at all. Second, if affirmation and negation were both true of everything indifferently, then all distinct things, a man, a wall, a ship, would collapse into one indistinguishable reality, since nothing could be truly said of one that could not equally be said of any other. Aquinas connects this directly to Protagoras's claim that whatever appears true to someone simply is true, and to Anaxagoras's doctrine that all things are mixed together, arguing that both dissolve the very possibility of determinate knowledge. Later, Aquinas develops what he treats as a distinct argument from degrees of falsity: even an opponent must admit that some errors lie closer to the truth than others, since claiming four equals five is less mistaken than claiming four equals a thousand, and this graded nearness to truth is unintelligible unless something is simply and unqualifiedly true. Throughout, Aquinas stresses that the denial of this principle, followed out consistently, would make rational speech, judgment, and purposeful action alike impossible.

Aquinas connects this chapter to the same root error examined earlier, tracing it now to two sources: the doctrine of Protagoras, that whatever seems true to a person simply is true, and a further argument drawn from observing nature itself. He explains that some thinkers were led to deny fixed truth through genuine philosophical difficulty, upon noticing that contrary qualities, hot and cold for instance, seem to arise out of one and the same underlying thing, which suggested to Anaxagoras and Democritus that opposites must already be present together beforehand. Aquinas resolves the puzzle by distinguishing potential from actual being: a thing can indeed be potentially both hot and cold at once, as lukewarm water is, but never actually both together, so the appearance of contradiction dissolves once potency and act are properly distinguished. He also notes Aristotle's appeal to an unchanging, immaterial reality as proof that not everything is caught up in such flux. Aquinas then surveys why sense experience misled Empedocles, Parmenides, Anaxagoras, and, in the poetic testimony of Homer's wounded Hector, why identifying knowledge outright with bodily sensation led these thinkers to conclude that truth itself shifts as the knower's bodily condition shifts. Aquinas rejects this by insisting that sensation is not identical with intellectual judgment, and that the object producing a sensation exists in itself prior to, and independently of, being sensed. He likewise turns aside the extreme Heraclitean position associated with Cratylus, who thought change so total that nothing could truly be named at all, by observing that even a changing subject retains something enduring throughout its change, and that only a small portion of the physical world, not the whole of reality, is actually subject to constant generation and decay.

Aquinas reads this chapter as Aristotle's answer to a further sophistical challenge: since perceptions and judgments differ between the sick and the healthy, the wise and the foolish, the sleeping and the waking, who has the right to say which perception is the true one? Aquinas observes that such questions, though posed as serious puzzles, are really no different from idly wondering whether one is presently asleep or awake, and that those who press this line demand a reason for everything, failing to see that not every truth needs, or even admits, demonstration; some truths are simply the starting points from which every demonstration must proceed. He explains Aristotle's central move: not everything that exists is relative to some perceiver's opinion, so the claim that whatever appears is true cannot stand in that unqualified form. One may only say that a thing appears true to a particular perceiver, in a particular respect, under particular conditions, at a particular time; once such qualifications are supplied, the apparent contradiction disappears, since what looks like honey to sight but not to taste involves two distinct judgments about two distinct respects, not one judgment contradicting itself. Aquinas adds that if everything truly depended on being perceived or thought, nothing could have existed before any perceiver did, which is plainly false. He closes by drawing out the conclusion toward which the whole discussion has been building: since contradictory statements cannot both be true of the same subject at once, neither can genuine contraries belong to the same subject at the same time and in the same respect, though they may belong to it in different respects, or one actually and the other only potentially.

Turning from the principle of non-contradiction to the closely related principle of excluded middle, Aquinas explains that Aristotle now argues no third possibility can stand between an affirmation and its contradictory negation: of any given subject, one must either truly assert or truly deny a given predicate, with nothing in between. Aquinas lays out several of Aristotle's proofs. From the very definitions of true and false: to say of what is that it is, or of what is not that it is not, is true, and nothing besides these two options is available, so any statement about a thing must be simply true or simply false. Aquinas also distinguishes two ways something might function as a middle term - one, like grey between black and white, sharing in both extremes within a common genus, and another, like a stone standing between man and horse, belonging to neither extreme and to no relevant common genus at all. He shows that neither kind of middle can be inserted between a contradictory affirmation and its negation: were it of the first sort, change could never pass directly between the two extremes without first passing through the middle, contrary to what is actually observed; were it of the second sort, no coherent account of change could be given at all. Aquinas notes that Aristotle traces the two mistaken positions back to their philosophical roots: Heraclitus's teaching that all things simultaneously are and are not tends to make everything true, while Anaxagoras's notion of a universal mixture, which posits a middle between contradictories, tends rather to make everything false, since a true mixture, being neither one extreme nor the other, cannot be accurately described by either.

In this closing chapter, Aquinas sees Aristotle gathering the threads of the whole book against two remaining extreme positions: that nothing whatsoever is true, and that everything without exception is true. Aquinas shows how each position collapses under its own weight the moment it is stated, since whoever claims that everything is true thereby affirms as true the further claim that his own view is false, and whoever claims that nothing is true thereby admits that his own claim is false as well. Even if such thinkers try to exempt their own assertion from the universal rule, Aquinas notes that Aristotle drives them into an unending regress of further exemptions, since calling one statement true generates the further true statement that it is true, and so on without limit. Aquinas traces both extreme positions back to Heraclitus, who held that all things are perpetually in motion, and follows Aristotle's rebuttal that if literally everything moved and nothing whatsoever remained fixed, nothing could be truly said of anything, since what is true already is the case, whereas what is merely coming to be is not yet; universal flux would thus produce, absurdly, universal falsehood. Yet Aquinas equally rejects the opposite extreme, that all things simply rest, since the truth-value of statements plainly does change over time, as when a person who now utters a sentence once did not exist to utter it. Aquinas closes by underscoring Aristotle's resolution: reality is neither wholly at rest nor wholly in motion, nor does everything merely alternate between the two, because there exists something always in motion and, beyond that, a first mover which is itself entirely unmoved - a conclusion Aquinas reads as pointing toward the higher, immaterial causes that first philosophy investigates more fully in the books that follow.
